title: Philanthropy Once Built Schools. Today, It Could Build a New Way to Learn Math ay-to-learn-math/
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman takes up Sarah Cone's question of why modern philanthropists no longer build, noting that Carnegie's libraries and Rosenwald's schools solved real scarcities that no longer exist. Today the barrier to learning is not access to schools or information but a time-based model that keeps same-age students in one room on one pace for 180 days. Math, he argues, suits a mastery model because content is sequenced and easy to assess, and research on acceleration supports letting students move ahead when ready. He proposes two linked investments: rigorous, independent AP-style math mastery assessments that give a common yardstick regardless of where a child learned, and school-based Math Labs where students advance on mastery with teachers acting as guides and fellows supporting. He admits it might fail, since students may need more human help or motivation, and recommends funding a serious evaluation to find out.
points: Access to books and schools is no longer the binding constraint, so ambitious philanthropy should target the time-based structure of schooling instead.
A trusted external mastery assessment would let a self-taught student's algebra be recognized by any school, solving the credentialing problem that blocks acceleration.
Math Labs would trade age-based classes for mastery-based progress, with credentialed teachers acting as guides and recent graduates serving as fellows.
Research synthesized over a century shows acceleration helps achievement, and cross-grade grouping by subject is especially relevant to math.
The proposal comes with an honest test plan: fund an evaluation of whether students who pass the assessments succeed in later courses and what adult support they need.
quotes: I think Cone is on to something. If a modern-day Carnegie or Rosenwald wanted to spend millions of dollars on a genuinely ambitious education project, what should he or she build?

But access to libraries and schools is no longer the main barrier to learning. Today, there are schools and libraries all over the country, and the internet has made information cheap and easy to access.

Schools aren’t designed to accommodate this abundance of information. They still put children of roughly the same age in a room and have a teacher deliver roughly the same material to all of them for the same 180 days.
A 2016 review synthesizing roughly a century of research found that academic acceleration had positive effects on student achievement.

Even if this student has mastered algebra, her school won’t necessarily recognize it. A parent can insist that her child already knows the material, but the school has no independent reason to believe it.

In exchange for shifting away from their time-based teaching method in math and letting students advance when they demonstrated mastery on the yardstick outlined above, the philanthropy would pay for the creation of Math Labs.
Rather than delivering, say, five lessons per day on seventh-grade math, they would work as a team to serve as math guides for students learning independently.

A philanthropist could fund a rigorous evaluation to test those assumptions, including whether students who passed the external assessments succeeded in subsequent courses and what kinds of adult support students need.
